article_title: US Charges Atlanta Activist for Using GrapheneOS Duress Password to Wipe Phone at Border
summary: Automated checks passed; manual source verification found a misattributed claim and a misspelled name in the body, both correctable via a public corrections note.

findings.message: Misattributed claim: article says 'border officers said they were demanding access to his phone "under the pretext of searching for child exploitation imagery"' but the TechCrunch snapshot attributes this framing to Tunick's attorneys' accusation against the government, not to a statement made by the officers themselves.
findings.details: TechCrunch snapshot (source-0.html.gz) reads: 'Tunick's attorneys accused the government of demanding access to his phone under the pretext of searching for child exploitation imagery, but without providing evidence to justify its suspicion.' The word 'pretext' is the attorneys' characterization, not something officers would self-report. The submission recasts this as officers' own statement, inverting who is making the claim. This is a body-level (What We Know section) misattribution, not present in the headline, summary, or Overview lead.

findings.message: Name misspelled: 'Bill Buddington' should be 'Bill Budington' (single 'd').
findings.details: TechCrunch snapshot spells the EFF technologist's name 'Bill Budington' ("Bill Budington, a senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation"). The submission body spells it 'Buddington' with a doubled 'd'. Minor but a factual/spelling error on a named source.

content_preview.title: US Charges Atlanta Activist for Using GrapheneOS Duress Password to Wipe Phone at Border
content_preview.summary: Federal prosecutors have charged Atlanta activist Samuel Tunick under a rarely used destruction-of-property statute for allegedly wiping his phone with GrapheneOS's duress password during a border search.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Federal prosecutors in the Northern District of Georgia have charged Samuel Tunick, an Atlanta-area activist, after he allegedly used a privacy feature built into GrapheneOS to wipe his phone during a border search, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/24/us-accuses-american-of-allegedly-wiping-his-phone-using-a-duress-password-during-border-search/). The case is thought to be the first known prosecution in the United States over the alleged destruction of data u...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece using the Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know format. Attribution phrases ('according to TechCrunch', 'Gizmodo reports') are used consistently throughout, and the 'What We Don't Know' section appropriately flags the unresolved penalty exposure, absence of a GrapheneOS developer statement, and the unresolved motion to suppress. Word count (634) is within the News category range (400-1200).
editor_notes.source_verification: Two sources cited, both on config/source_allowlist.txt (techcrunch.com, gizmodo.com). SOURCE 1 (TechCrunch, source-0.html.gz, sha256 0796ae3f...fb0f9, verified by re-gunzip+rehash match against manifest.json): read in full as plain text. Confirms: the January 24, 2025 Hartsfield-Jackson secondary-inspection encounter; GrapheneOS duress-passcode mechanism; the verbatim quote 'the screen went blank, flashed several times and the phone appeared to restart'; Matthew Dodge's role and 'incredibly rare' characterization (paraphrased faithfully as 'rare' in the submission); the verbatim Runa Sandvik quotes (both sentences match exactly); the 'first known case' framing; and the federal statute description (destruction of property to prevent seizure). Also surfaced a MISATTRIBUTION (see findings): the submission attributes the 'pretext of searching for child exploitation imagery' framing to 'border officers,' but TechCrunch attributes this framing to an accusation made BY Tunick's attorneys AGAINST the government -- an inversion of who is speaking. Also surfaced a NAME MISSPELLING: TechCrunch spells the EFF technologist 'Bill Budington'; submission spells it 'Bill Buddington.' SOURCE 2 (Gizmodo, source-1.html.gz, sha256 64d0b21d...232f84, verified by re-gunzip+rehash match against manifest.json): decompressing and reading this snapshot revealed IT DOES NOT CONTAIN THE CITED GIZMODO ARTICLE. Despite manifest.json reporting status_code 200, content_type text/html, and error: null for this entry, the actual saved HTML is a Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) capture of an unrelated Medical Xpress story ('Death of girl in Chinese gene-editing trial kept secret: Report', canonical URL https://web.archive.org/web/20260726173239/https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-07-death-girl-chinese-gene-trial.html) -- a completely different topic (a Chinese gene-editing trial death), not the GrapheneOS/Tunick story at all. This is a snapshot-capture failure in the pipeline's fetcher (likely a caching/URL-routing bug in the archive-fallback path), not a reviewer oversight -- I verified the sha256 of the decompressed file matches the manifest's recorded hash, so the manifest and file are internally consistent; the fetcher simply saved the wrong page under this filename. Per the skill's fallback procedure for a failed/unusable snapshot, I performed a live WebFetch of the actual cited URL (https://gizmodo.com/a-feature-that-makes-your-phone-data-self-destruct-in-authorities-hands-may-soon-have-its-day-in-court-2000790831) as a last resort. That live fetch confirmed: the exact statutory citation 'Title 18, United States Code, Section 2232(a)'; the verbatim indictment text reproduced in the submission ('did knowingly destroy, damage, waste, dispose of, and otherwise take any action to delete the digital contents of a Google Pixel cellular phone, for the purpose of preventing and impairing the Government's lawful authority to take said property into its custody and control') including the 'Northern District of Georgia' venue and the 'L.C.' officer identifier; the verbatim Christophe Boutry quote ('sends the message that [GrapheneOS] is criminal by default'); the verbatim Marlon Kautz quote ('We all have a right to secure our private data against unconstitutional searches. And we should - especially in a time of rising authoritarianism.'); the GiveSendGo fundraiser detail that Tunick was arrested roughly ten months later during a traffic stop over a tail-light issue by FBI/DHS officers; and that Gizmodo itself independently describes Tunick as an 'Atlanta-based activist' with ties to the 'Stop Cop City'/Defend the Atlanta Forest movement, which supports the headline's 'Atlanta Activist' framing even though TechCrunch alone does not use that word. I am flagging the broken source-1 snapshot explicitly so it can be re-fetched/repaired in the provenance record; the corrections note below covers the two content-level issues found, not the snapshot bug itself (which is a pipeline/infrastructure issue, not a content fabrication).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All specific facts, dates, statutory citations, and direct quotes verified against source content (TechCrunch snapshot directly, Gizmodo via live WebFetch after its snapshot proved corrupted) check out, with two exceptions: (1) the 'border officers said... under the pretext of' framing inverts the actual attribution (it was Tunick's attorneys' accusation, per TechCrunch), and (2) 'Bill Buddington' is misspelled ('Budington' is correct). Both are subordinate, body-level details; neither affects the headline, summary, or Overview lead, all of which are independently well-supported.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. No sensationalism, no editorializing, no AI self-reference. Quotes from advocacy-aligned sources (EFF, Atlanta Solidarity Fund) are clearly attributed as such rather than presented as neutral fact, and the piece includes the government's declined-to-comment status.
editor_notes.originality: No existing article in src/content/articles/ or src/content/article-meta/ mentions Tunick, GrapheneOS, or a duress-wipe border case (grep across both trees returned no hits). This is new-topic coverage, not a duplicate.
concerns: Body misattributes the 'pretext of searching for child exploitation imagery' framing to border officers when TechCrunch sources it to an accusation by Tunick's defense attorneys.

The Gizmodo source snapshot committed to provenance (source-1.html.gz) does not actually contain the Gizmodo article -- it is a mis-saved, unrelated Wayback Machine capture of a different story. This should be re-fetched before/after merge so the provenance record's snapshot matches its manifest description; I verified the correct facts via live WebFetch in the meantime.
recommendations: Re-run the source snapshot fetcher for the Gizmodo URL so provenance/sources/2026-07/<slug>/source-1.html.gz contains the actual cited article rather than an unrelated Medical Xpress capture.
In a future edit or corrigenda, correct 'Bill Buddington' to 'Bill Budington' and correct the attribution of the 'pretext' framing to Tunick's attorneys rather than to border officers.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively accurate, well-sourced News piece on a genuinely novel legal story. Headline, summary, and lead are all solidly supported by the sources. Two minor, body-level issues (an attribution inversion and a name misspelling) are honestly covered by a public corrections note; neither undermines the article's central thesis. Publishing with corrections is appropriate; REJECT is not warranted since no fabricated event, unsourced lead, or provenance-breaking orphan URL was found, and the pattern is two isolated slips rather than systemic fabrication. Separately, the Gizmodo source snapshot itself needs to be re-fetched as a pipeline/infrastructure fix -- this is independent of the article's content quality.
